title: Who Wrote the Menu?
evidence_boundary: The restaurant, casino, and streaming-service comparisons are metaphors for constrained political choice and institutional power. The script does not claim that voting is meaningless, elections are predetermined, or every political system operates identically.
desired_movement: From equating ballot choice with complete control to examining who defines the available options, while preserving the value of voting and other forms of participation.
grounding: The ordinary menu, table, meal, kitchen, and shrinking portion keep the analysis anchored in familiar daily life.
invitation: When a political menu is handed to you, what would you ask about the kitchen?
end_card_question: When they hand you the menu, what would you ask about the kitchen?
political_visual_boundary: No real candidate likenesses, party logos, campaign slogans, flags used as partisan identifiers, or claims about a specific election. Red and blue are used only as abstract plate colors from the supplied metaphor.
voice_standard: Liam — warm, sly, lucid, and slightly incredulous; dry humor around the dinner argument, lower and more intimate on the structural questions, nearly a whisper on the final reveal.

scenes.text: They hand you a menu every few years and call it power. Two entrees. Red plate. Blue plate. Pick one.
scenes.semantic_anchor: two-option menu presented as power

scenes.text: Then everybody starts arguing across the table like the fate of civilization depends on whether the chicken came with mashed potatoes or rice.
scenes.semantic_anchor: diners arguing over nearly identical meals
scenes.query: group of people arguing across a restaurant table over two similar chicken dinners, one with mashed potatoes and one with rice, animated gestures and napkins, no party logos, no politicians, genuine motion

scenes.text: Meanwhile, nobody is allowed in the kitchen. You did not choose the ingredients. You did not hire the cooks.
scenes.semantic_anchor: customers excluded from the kitchen
scenes.query: closed restaurant kitchen door and frosted glass threshold while ingredient crates and cooks move behind it, visible separation between dining room and kitchen, no logos, real motion

scenes.text: You did not select the suppliers. You did not set the prices. You did not decide who owns the building.
scenes.semantic_anchor: supply trucks, price board, and ownership keys controlled elsewhere
scenes.query: delivery crates arrive at a restaurant back entrance, metal keys turn in a lock, invoices and a price scale move across a manager desk, no readable brands, real motion

scenes.text: But because someone placed a menu in your hand, you are told the restaurant belongs to you. That is the illusion.
scenes.semantic_anchor: menu mistaken for ownership

scenes.text: Political choice is often presented as control, when sometimes it is only participation inside boundaries you never agreed to.
scenes.semantic_anchor: choice inside a prebuilt dining boundary
scenes.query: arrows and route lines move between two marked paths on a restaurant floor plan while fixed barriers and velvet ropes block every other direction, no political logos, real motion

scenes.text: You are free to choose. As long as you choose from what has already been chosen for you.
scenes.semantic_anchor: two visible options and many hidden ones
scenes.image_prompt: photoreal restaurant menu open to only two illuminated dishes while many other covered dishes sit behind a locked kitchen pass, elegant cinematic light, strong depth, visual clarity, no readable text, no party symbols, no people required

scenes.text: And the menu is designed carefully. Not just to feed you. To divide the table.

scenes.query: movable wall unfolds from a long restaurant menu and divides one shared dining room table into red-lit and blue-lit halves, food remains similar, no logos, genuine motion

scenes.text: One side is told the other side wants to poison the meal. The other side is told your side is trying to shut down the restaurant.
scenes.semantic_anchor: two sides receiving conflicting warnings

scenes.text: Now everybody is yelling, throwing napkins, and accusing strangers of destroying dinner while the owner quietly raises the prices.

scenes.query: group of diners yell and throw napkins across a busy restaurant while a calm owner in the background quietly raises a price board, no readable numbers, no political logos, real motion

scenes.text: And somehow, after every election, the kitchen gets bigger, the dining room gets louder, and the people eating are still asking why the portions keep shrinking.

scenes.image_prompt: cinematic photoreal restaurant cross-section with wall calendar pages flipping through repeated years, an industrial kitchen expanding behind glass, a louder crowded dining room, and tiny portions on large plates, dramatic scale contrast, deep perspective, no logos, no politicians, no readable text

scenes.text: That does not mean your vote has no value. It means a vote is not the entire structure.

scenes.query: single printed ballot-like choice card placed carefully beside a large restaurant architectural floor plan and operating manual, pages turn to reveal the wider structure, no party logos, no candidate names, real motion

scenes.text: Choosing the meal is not the same as deciding how the restaurant operates. Real power asks deeper questions.

scenes.text: Who writes the menu? Who funds the kitchen?

scenes.text: Who benefits when the customers hate each other more than they question the management?

scenes.text: Because a system can offer choice and still control the range of outcomes.

scenes.text: A casino lets you choose the machine. That does not mean you own the casino.
